title: The Yellow Wallpaper
focus: confinement driving a woman into madness

teacherSummary.text: A woman recovering from what her physician husband John calls a 'temporary nervous depression' after childbirth keeps a secret journal during a summer 'rest cure' in an old mansion. Forbidden to write or work, she is confined to a nursery with barred windows and hideous yellow wallpaper. She comes to see a woman trapped behind its pattern. On the last night she tears the paper off to free her, identifies with her, and creeps around the room; John faints at the sight.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Yellow Wallpaper,” how does Gilman show confinement driving a woman into madness? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Yellow Wallpaper, how does Gilman develop the idea of confinement driving a woman into madness? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the point of view in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Yellow Wallpaper develops the idea of confinement driving a woman into madness. writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Yellow Wallpaper (where it begins, turns and ends) and its point of view shape the reader's understanding of confinement driving a woman into madness. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Yellow Wallpaper suggests about confinement driving a woman into madness. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's point of view and symbolism), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Charlotte Perkins Gilman uses point of view in The Yellow Wallpaper to complicate the reader's understanding of confinement driving a woman into madness. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Yellow Wallpaper within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of confinement driving a woman into madness responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Yellow Wallpaper alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of confinement driving a woman into madness follows or bends those conventions, using the point of view as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Yellow Wallpaper and its treatment of confinement driving a woman into madness. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's point of view and symbolism, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Yellow Wallpaper as evidence for a larger claim about confinement driving a woman into madness in The Yellow Wallpaper. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Yellow Wallpaper as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of confinement driving a woman into madness. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Yellow Wallpaper.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the story for point of view, symbolism (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this story suggest about confinement driving a woman into madness? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how The Yellow Wallpaper develops the idea of confinement driving a woman into madness. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The narrator's madness is a response to her confinement. When the text says “There are things in that paper that nobody knows but me” (The Yellow Wallpaper, paragraph 120), it shows this directly. Early, she remarks that "John laughs at me, of course, but one expects that in marriage"; forbidden to work, she fixes on the paper ("There are things in that paper that nobody knows but me") and finally claims "I’ve got out at last," freedom found only in madness.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the story to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Sensitive content: Postpartum depression and psychosis; controlling marriage. Preview the story, tell students in advance, and allow a pass on reading aloud. Keep discussion on how the writer uses these elements, not on graphic detail.
contentNotes.studentPreview: Heads-up: this story includes postpartum depression and psychosis; controlling marriage. Support is available if this is hard to read.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Why does the writer include this, and what does it make us notice?”

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
safeMessaging.studentResource: If you or someone you know is struggling or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, U.S.) or talk with a school counselor today.
safeMessaging.counselorPrompt: Let a counselor know in advance that this story is being taught.
